query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature exposure in oxidizing atmospheres, the reactive elements (notably Ti and Al) in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA preferentially oxidize along grain boundaries, forming brittle oxide precipitates that degrade grain boundary cohesion. This degradation mechanism leads to intergranular embrittlement and ultimately catastrophic failure, whereas exposure in reducing conditions suppresses such oxidation and delays failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix that exhibits a relatively homogenous distribution of elements and minimal pre-existing oxide precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subjecting samples to controlled high-temperature exposure (e.g. around 700°C) under different gas atmospheres, specifically comparing an oxidizing environment (e.g. pure O2 or air) with a reducing environment (e.g. H2-diluted inert gas).
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (approximately 700°C) for extended periods (e.g., 100 hours) in environments with well-defined oxygen partial pressures (oxidizing vs. reducing conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and associated intergranular regions where selective oxidation leads to precipitate formation.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of reactive species (Ti and Al) at grain boundaries forms brittle oxides (such as TiO2 and Al2O3). These precipitates weaken the cohesion along grain boundaries, introducing stress concentration sites that lead to crack initiation and intergranular failure, which under loading conditions can cause catastrophic fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing exposure, one would observe an increased number and size of oxide precipitates at grain boundaries as well as a reduction in ductility and toughness relative to the baseline. In contrast, samples exposed to reducing conditions should show a suppressed formation of these oxide phases and retain more of their original mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy, characterized by a uniform FCC matrix with minimal oxide content and robust grain boundary integrity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for exposures around 700°C and may not hold at significantly lower temperatures or in gas atmospheres that are not clearly oxidizing or reducing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact identities, morphologies, and spatial distributions of the oxide precipitates remain uncertain, and additional factors such as diffusion kinetics and possible internal oxidation may also influence degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the additively manufactured alloy. Expose one set to a controlled oxidizing environment (e.g., air or pure O2) and another set to a reducing environment (e.g., an inert carrier with a small percentage of H2) at 700°C for 100 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural characterization focusing on grain boundary oxidation (using TEM/SEM and XRD) and evaluate mechanical properties (tensile testing for ductility and toughness).
measurements: Grain boundary imaging to identify and quantify oxide precipitates
X-ray diffraction to confirm the presence of phases such as TiO2/Al2O3
Tensile and fracture toughness tests to measure degradation in mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed in the oxidizing environment do not exhibit a significant increase in brittle oxide precipitates at grain boundaries and if their mechanical properties (ductility, toughness) are not markedly degraded relative to samples in the reducing environment, the hypothesis that selective intergranular oxidation governs catastrophic failure is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
